articles.title: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.

articles.title: Reading, Writing and Repairing Game-Theoretic Policies in Weight Space
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a language model work in the weight space of a policy network for a repeated game? We put four questions to a mid-size open model, on recurrent networks of 1{,}218 weights with exactly checkable answers. Given a population of opponents described in English, write a policy that is optimal: its value is a finite computation over the agent's information state, so a submitted network has an exact gap from the optimum. Given a network's weights, report its action after each of fifteen opponent histories; recover the state machine it implements, judged on every opponent sequence to depth ten; or repair a network whose output was altered in one place and say which round first goes wrong. The model recovers the program in 62 of 66 replies, reports all fifteen behavioral entries correctly in 34 of 36, and attains the optimum in 20 of 20 when it states a policy the evaluator compiles. Repair is the exception: 4 of 18 repaired, 5 of 18 diagnosed, with a median patch covering one of the two entries needed.

articles.title: ADE: A Zero-Training Unlearning Method for Latent World Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent world models learn compact recurrent dynamics from offline trajectories, yet deployed simulators can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions from outdated physical regimes. Existing unlearning methods fail in autoregressive physics: gradient updates distort latent manifolds and compound rollout drift, naive output zeroing suppresses valid control responses on trigger onset, and single-step deletion leaves corruption inside recurrent hidden states. We propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm for latent world models. Using only cached pretraining moments, ADE recovers retain covariances via single-pass matrix downdating without raw retain data and cascades closed-form edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states, and downstream heads. Pairing orthogonal excision with whitened recurrent damping and mean-preserving affine calibration neutralizes out-of-manifold backdoors and realigns in-manifold shifts without variance collapse. Across four regimes on three MuJoCo benchmarks, ADE outperforms seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1, eliminating HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers $4.4\times$ faster than fine-tuning, and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.

articles.title: Calm Agent: Reframing Agent Interaction around Intermittent Human Attention
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32009v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces. We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

articles.title: To Critic Or Not To Critic
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models tackle longer and more complex tasks, understanding when a critic improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes increasingly important. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains a critic to reduce variance and provide fine-grained credit assignment, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) drops the critic and avoids the bias of bootstrapping from the critic's value estimates. Although recent critic-based methods have reported strong performance relative to GRPO, it remains unclear when each approach is preferable. We argue that there is no universal answer; instead, the choice depends on several interacting factors, including batch size, critic reliance, and task complexity. We study the bias-variance tradeoff in terms of gradient direction, measuring how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows. Under a shared actor objective, we compare GRPO with PPO in control tasks, short-horizon math, and long-horizon terminal agents. Across more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with LLMs, we find that PPO generally leads at small batch sizes, while GRPO often overtakes heavily bootstrapped PPO and reaches parity with lightly bootstrapped PPO at larger batches. At longer horizons and in more complex domains, GRPO needs larger batches to catch up to PPO's performance. Accounting for training compute, critics pay off at small budgets, but their returns diminish at larger budgets.

articles.title: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are tuned once and frozen, although the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. We study whether an online learner can pick these settings at runtime. AdaptR4j swaps Resilience4j policies atomically in Spring Boot 3 and lets a contextual bandit choose among complete CircuitBreaker/Retry/Bulkhead configurations from Prometheus signals. Our first, naive design scored worse than keeping the default policy in three of four winnable fault scenarios under the reward it optimised: exploring a menu that contained aggressive circuit breakers rejected most traffic while the learner was still learning. Two safeguards fix this: a safe policy menu (no breaker stricter than the latency SLO) and safe exploration with a bounded reward. With them, AdaptR4j beats the production default in every winnable scenario (p < 0.001, three runs each, run-to-run SD < = 0.03), beats the best fixed policy when the fault changes over time, and cuts user-visible failures up to 3.7x compared with the naive design. A context-free bandit on the same safe menu performs statistically indistinguishably, so the safeguards - not the learner - carry most of the benefit. We also report how an earlier version of our harness produced convincing but wrong results: a unit mismatch made every circuit breaker 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to the metrics, so 94% of user requests failed while latency and error metrics looked excellent.

articles.title: Structure-Aware Transformers for Hierarchical Authorization in Personal AI Agents
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personal AI agents can carry out complex, multi-step tasks on users' behalf, but doing so often involves numerous permission requests. Manually reviewing each request is time-consuming, while indiscriminate approval poses privacy and security risks. Predicting users' authorization preferences offers a way to reduce this burden while preserving user control. However, authorization prediction is challenging because permission requests are often hierarchical and observed user decisions are sparse and potentially correlated. To address these challenges, We propose the Parent-gated Authorization Transformer for Hierarchies (PATH) to predict users' authorization preferences for personal AI agents. PATH is a novel neural network architecture that combines hierarchy-aware attention masks with a parent-gated probability formulation to ensure hierarchy-consistent predictions. Hierarchy-level embeddings further support learning from sparse observations and patterns shared within each authorization level. We establish finite-sample risk bounds and provide sufficient conditions for consistent authorization probability estimation and algorithmic convergence. Experiments on simulated data, AI-generated user profiles, and real user authorization data demonstrate strong predictive performance with zero hierarchy violations.

articles.title: HuluOPD: Unifying Heterogeneous Medical Specialists into One Lightweight Model with Unlabeled Prompts
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32021v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.

articles.title: Beyond Before-and-After Images: Evaluating Temporal Grounding in a Lightweight VLM for Disaster Assessment
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bi-temporal satellite imagery is central to disaster assessment: deciding what was damaged requires comparing a pre-event scene with its post-event counterpart. A vision-language model (VLM) can nonetheless appear to answer change questions while relying mainly on the post-event image or on the prompt's temporal framing. We present a controlled diagnostic of temporal grounding and apply it to one lightweight VLM, InternVL3-2B, on DisasterM3: 1,659 optical and SAR image pairs from 41 events and nine disaster types, in event-disjoint partitions, with 9,031 reasoning questions. We compare post-only input, the true pre/post pair, the post image repeated twice, reversed image order, and an unrelated pre-event image. The true pair scores $+0.5$ accuracy points above the repeated-post control (95\% paired bootstrap CI $[-0.2, +1.2]$), and reversing the order changes accuracy by $-0.2$ points ($[-0.8, +0.5]$). Under this protocol we therefore find no measurable benefit from the content of the true pre-event image and little sensitivity to temporal order. The model is not blind to the first image, however: the true pair scores $2.5$ points above a pair whose pre-event image comes from another event ($[+1.6, +3.4]$). State-transition and multi-hop questions remain hard, and optical and SAR inputs show different profiles. We outline temporal scene graphs as a testable next step, not a validated solution, and argue that temporal benchmarks for Earth observation should report whether answers depend on the intended evidence, not only how often they are right.

articles.title: Do Occupancy World Models Really Follow Actions?
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Occupancy world models predict future 3D scenes conditioned on ego actions, yet their predictions may not faithfully follow the specified trajectory under counterfactual actions. Because driving datasets provide sparse coverage of alternative trajectories for each scene, existing models learn the spatial effect of ego motion implicitly from observed scene--trajectory combinations, which may entangle action effects with scene--trajectory correlations. We propose ReCast, an ego-trajectory-guided transformer that grounds future prediction in action-induced geometric correspondence across ego-centric frames. ReCast decouples historical encoding from future decoding and aligns deformable interactions using relative ego transformations, while retaining flexibility for non-rigid scene evolution. We also introduce a counterfactual action-faithfulness benchmark covering in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories. On Occ3D-nuScenes, ReCast achieves competitive standard forecasting performance while improving counterfactual forecasting, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution trajectories.

articles.title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32031v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it

articles.title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement. Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. articles.title: Spec-CoFrGeNet: Reparametrizing Continued Fraction Networks for Stable and Accurate Training
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continued fractions have been shown to be a function class capable of constructing expressive yet parameter-efficient neural networks. These neural networks are not only effective for supervised learning, but also for training LLMs. However, the rational form of this function class introduces poles when the denominator approaches zero, which prior work has avoided by enforcing a small positive (non-smooth) lower bound. We show that performance and training stability can be highly sensitive to the choice of this lower bound. In this work, we introduce a novel transformation of the partial denominators, inspired by its connection to the Green's function in physics, that mitigates the above issue elegantly by constraining the spectra of the constructed tridiagonal Hamiltonian. Our approach further eliminates the need for incremental training used by previous works for stability, thus avoiding involved modifications to standard pre-training procedures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our reparameterization by replacing FFNs with a previously proposed continued fraction architecture for both language and image generative modeling. Across diverse models, such as GPT-2 XL, (nano) Llama-MoE, and Granite, we show that our proposed method achieves performance comparable to the original (FFN-based) architectures while maintaining ~30%-50% parameter savings as before, and in most cases even outperforms the more complicated incremental training baseline. We further demonstrate, for the first time for continued fraction networks, that their effectiveness also carries over to image generative modeling, that utilize diffusion objectives. On a state-of-the-art Diffusion Transformer, we show that our approach again achieves performance

articles.title: Integral DeltaNet: Improved Linear Attention with Adaptive Memory Integration
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.32063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.

articles.title: Local subspace encoding for spectral prediction: from TabPFN to operator-adaptive calibration
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: TabPFN has already shown useful predictive performance on near-infrared spectra. RamanPFN subsequently proposed two spectral representations for tabular inference: Global Compositional Unmixing (GCU) and Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding (LVSE). We assess whether these representations also help on datasets assembled through the nirs4all ecosystem, and whether their value extends to classical calibration. We reanalyse completed experiments from a public spectral dataset catalogue. On a post-hoc subset of 61 matched numerical prediction tasks, after excluding ten class-code, metadata or semantically ambiguous targets, LVSE reduces RMSE relative to raw-spectrum TabPFN by 10.22%, 12.80% and 14.52% on average for checkpoints 2.5, 3 and 3.5, respectively, with median reductions of 4.99%, 4.74% and 7.82%. Across 76 classification datasets, weighted F1 increases by 2.22, 2.56 and 3.81 percentage points. The 2.5 classification procedure uses output coding on 15 datasets exceeding the checkpoint's native class limit. GCU alone is less reliable in this implementation. LVSE also improves PLS and Ridge in many cases, with median RMSE reductions of 4.75% and 1.89%. Adding LVSE candidates to an operator-adaptive model is feasible, but a separate 35-task panel derived from the public AOM benchmark shows only small median gains. These results motivate evaluating LVSE alongside existing representation choices. They do not establish that a selector choosing between raw and LVSE inputs will improve every task.

articles.title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) allows language models to verbalise multi-step rationales before producing their final answer. While this technique often boosts task performance and offers an impression of transparency into the model's reasoning, this position paper argues that rationales generated by current CoT techniques can be misleading and are neither necessary nor sufficient for trustworthy interpretability. We analyse faithfulness as whether CoTs are not only human-interpretable but also reflect the model's underlying reasoning well enough to support responsible use. By synthesising evidence from prior work, we systematically show that verbalised chains are frequently unfaithful, diverging from the critical hidden computations that drive a model's predictions. As CoT is increasingly relied upon in application domains, including high-stakes ones such as medicine, law, and autonomous systems, we further argue that this unfaithfulness is not taken seriously enough in these settings: our analysis of 1,000 recent CoT-centric papers finds that approximately 21.7% explicitly treat CoT as a load-bearing interpretability technique, building pipelines or safety arguments that would not hold if CoT is unfaithful to the model's actual reasoning. They include papers in high-stakes domains that heavily hinge on such interpretability claims. Building on prior work, we make three proposals: (i) avoid treating CoT as being sufficient for interpretability without additional verification, (ii) adopt rigorous methods that assess faithfulness for downstream decision-making, and (iii) report such assessments alongside any interpretability claims based on CoT, while continuing to use CoT for its communicative and monitoring benefits.

articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: WM-811K (also known as LSWMD) is a wafer map dataset first made publicly available in a 2015 paper by Wu et al. Convolutional neural networks have been used to achieve high classification accuracy on this dataset, yet it's not easy to decipher which features of the dataset are driving that performance. This study attempts to answer this specifically for WM-811K: how much of the predictive performance results from the wafer layout, the count of failed dies, their distance from the center and their exact 2-D location. After analyzing duplicate wafer maps, removing same wafer maps with conflicting labels and ensuring that the same manufacturing lot or exact same map doesn't appear in training, validation and test data, we were left with 25,513 defect-labeled wafer maps from eight classes. We then constructed four variations of each wafer map. The Original was the actual wafer map present in the dataset. The Layout-only kept only the layout of the non-background dies. The Global-shuffle kept the count of failed dies while shuffling them around. The Radial-shuffle randomized the locations of failed dies only in their radial bin, which was chosen out of 8 radial bins based on distance from the center. The data split, preprocessing and CNN architecture remained the same for all four of them. Macro-F1 progressed like this: 0.3829 (Layout-only), 0.5803 (Global-shuffle), 0.7439 (Radial-shuffle) and 0.8563 (Original). These results show that WM-811K contains useful information at several levels: wafer layout, number of failures, distribution of failed dies in a given radius, and exact 2-D locations of the failed dies. articles.title: Flagging Batch Shift in Flow Cytometry using Jeffreys Divergence between Gaussian Mixtures
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning models for clinical flow cytometry are usually evaluated on data drawn from their training distribution. In routine practice, however, acquisition conditions and reagents may change, potentially making predictions unreliable without warning. We propose a model agnostic criterion for prediction reliability based on a notion of distance from the training distribution: each patient sample is represented by a Gaussian mixture model, and its Jeffreys divergence to a reference fitted on the training data is estimated using Monte Carlo integration. We illustrate our approach on real-life shifted cohorts of acute myeloid leukaemia patients, using a classifier trained to predict NPM1 mutation status. First, we show graphically and statistically that pairwise divergences capture acquisition cohort structure. We then calibrate a rejection threshold on a subset of shifted cohort samples and evaluate it on held-out subjects. Across 20 runs, the misclassification rate of rejected samples was 2.5 times larger than for retained samples. These results suggest that input divergence can help identify unreliable predictions, providing a strong candidate component for abstention frameworks, along with quality control measures and classifier confidence.

articles.title: Fusion Gains Depend on the Implementation and the Calibration Target: An 18-Task Study of Prediction Intervals with a Single-Source Fallback
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A fused model can benefit from an extra learning stage as well as from a second data source. We compare four fusion implementations with matched single-source learners on 18 regression tasks with prediction intervals. Across ten refits under group-wise calibration, linear stacking improved the interval score by 6.0% against a source model without a second stage and by 0.1% against its matched single source. The four implementations agreed on 3 of 18 tasks and gave opposite clear verdicts on 12, including 8 of the 10 tasks with naturally distinct sources. With pointwise calibration, they agreed on 5 tasks and gave opposite clear verdicts on 9. A development-set selector with a matched single-source fallback improved ten-refit task-averaged scores by 2.2--6.3% in every implementation under both calibrations. Adding fused arms to the pool of single-source candidates improved the mean relative score by about 5 percentage points. Under group-wise calibration, the gradient-boosted selector met the criterion frozen before evaluation on eight held-out tasks. In post-opening refits, selectors lost to the matched single source in 4.4--6.1% of task-level runs under group-wise calibration. Under signed pointwise calibration, three implementations lost in 19--23% of runs. Fusion evaluations should compare matched candidates on held-out data and report how often the selector loses alongside its average gain.

articles.title: Detecting Harmful Short Videos in Toxic Diet Culture: A Governance-Ready Evidence Framework with Sparse Autoencoders
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algorithmic content moderation is increasingly important for governing short-form video content, yet harmful-content detection research focuses primarily on prediction or limited explanations. This leaves a governance challenge underexplored: producing decision-linked evidence that supports the review and justification of moderation decisions. Using toxic diet culture as an empirical case, we conceptualize governance-ready evidence as computational traceability, evidence localization, policy grounding, and evidence inspectability. We develop the Sparse Autoencoder-based Policy-Aligned Contrastive Evidence (SPACE) framework in a pretrained SAE feature space derived from a large multimodal model. A global relevance gate and decomposable linear evidence head identify decision-linked evidence; segment supervision and within-video ranking localize this evidence; policy alignment maps it to platform guidelines; and Pareto-efficient selection yields a compact, task-specific evidence vocabulary. On 3,711 labeled TikTok videos, SPACE achieves the highest harmful-category Macro F1 among benchmarks across four families, at 0.8507. Its highest-scoring observation overlaps a ground-truth harmful span for 88.0% of harmful test videos, while its evidence representation retrieves the corresponding policy category for 87.0%. Stakeholder evaluations indicate that the SPACE evidence report is perceived as useful for understanding, reviewing, documenting, and responding to moderation decisions. The study contributes computational design science knowledge for embedding governance-ready evidence within predictive content-moderation systems.

articles.title: CaLA: Causal Latent Adjustment for World Models under Adaptive Policies
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models is answering ``imagine" answers to ``what-if'' questions via imagined rollouts. But rollouts collected by adaptive policies induce treatment-outcome confounding in imagined rollouts. We study this problem in Match-3 difficulty adjustment, where latent player skill influences both assigned difficulty and churn. We build a fully specified Match-3 SCM with sequential mechanics, adaptive assignment, and paired ground-truth interventions, on which unadjusted models fit to the logged trajectories select difficulty settings that raise churn. We then introduce Causal Latent Adjustment (CaLA), a DAG-constrained world model that infers a variational player representation from pretreatment history. Across our evaluations, CaLA provides the most reliable population-level intervention estimates and competitive individualized decisions, although rich handcrafted histories can remain advantageous for individual-level adjustment. We further find that residual correction can degrade causal decision quality despite improving predictive fit, highlighting the need to distinguish predictive accuracy, confounding adjustment and the behavior of downstream causal estimators.

articles.title: Is 4 Bits Enough for EEG Sleep Staging? A Subject-Level Benchmark of MXFP4, NVFP4 and FP8
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Staging sleep on a wearable device keeps the raw electroencephalogram (EEG) private and saves the energy needed to transmit it. It also requires small, energy-efficient neural networks. We benchmark 13 post-training quantization (PTQ) configurations, from FP16 to the block-scaled 4-bit formats MXFP4 and NVFP4, for five-stage sleep staging from single-channel Fpz-Cz EEG. We use Sleep-EDF-78 (78 subjects), subject-wise cross-validation, three training seeds, value-exact emulation, and per-subject paired statistics. All 8- and 16-bit formats stay within 0.45 percentage points (pp) of FP32 Macro-F1. With 4-bit weights and activations, an epoch-wise CNN loses 1.98 to 3.04 pp, and a temporal-context network loses at most 1.19 pp. A same-encoder ablation shows that temporal context explains little of this gap. At equal block size, NVFP4 outperforms MXFP4. The first layer, which quantizes the raw EEG, is the most sensitive layer in both networks. Keeping the first and last layers in FP8 brings both tested 4-bit formats within 0.48 pp of FP32. This recipe adds at most 2.1% weight storage, needs no retraining, and is equivalent to quantization-aware training (QAT) within an exploratory 1-pp margin. The 4-bit losses fall on the same subjects across architectures (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.69 to 0.79), and they reduce N3 recall the most. On the nested Sleep-EDF-20 subset, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers again stays within 0.25 pp of FP32. Under MXFP4, however, the ranking of the architectures reverses, and FP8 first and last layers do not fully recover two of the three tested models. In our emulation, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers thus loses little accuracy without QAT in both cohorts.

articles.title: Transformers with Signatures: Towards Universal In-Context Learning in Path Space
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general, and elusive in particular when target responses depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Building on the universal linear approximation property of signatures, we construct explicitly a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query. Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.

First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). articles.title: Transferable, Time-Parallel Graph Dynamics via Space-Time Factorization
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-parallel neural operators (FNO and successors) have transformed PDE surrogates on regular grids. Mesh-based operators (MeshGraphNets, Transolver) extend operator learning to irregular geometries, but jointly learning across diverse topologies while retaining non-recurrent temporal evaluation remains challenging. We propose space-time factorization: partition the model into local temporal operators (learned, graph-independent) and a spatial mixer that propagates information across nodes without graph-dependent learned parameters. This structural condition lets the same parameters run on unseen graphs; non-recurrent instances also admit time-parallel evaluation. Accurate zero-shot transfer further depends on controlling three information leaks (graph-dependent weights, graph-specific features, and graph-correlated training distributions) and on suitable task physics and training coverage. The protocol applies to two distinct spatial-mixer families, fixed-spectral and learned-attention. We validate the principle in three domains. articles.title: SwiftLoop: Selective Refinement for Adaptive Implicit Reasoning in Looped Transformers
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Looped Transformers advance implicit chain-of-thought reasoning through recurrent latent refinement. However, existing looped reasoners typically employ fixed-depth recurrence, updating all latent positions at every iteration and incurring redundancy when further refinement is unnecessary. We introduce \textsc{SwiftLoop}, an inference-time framework for selective recurrent refinement through position-wise freezing, enabling adaptive computation allocation across both recurrent depth and active width. SwiftLoop learns lightweight freezing policies through hindsight-guided supervision derived from two complementary criteria: K/V reusability at the internal representation level and functional impact at the output level. At inference time, these policies guide adaptive freezing based on observed hidden states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SwiftLoop achieves favorable accuracy--computation trade-offs over fixed-loop inference and adaptive baselines, with measured inference acceleration. Beyond implicit reasoning, we further demonstrate its applicability to recurrent prompt prefilling in general looped models.

articles.title: CHORD: Learning Latent Spaces for Constrained Stellarator Design
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In high-dimensional, PDE-constrained design, interpolating between known feasible solutions can reveal trade-offs without repeating expensive optimization campaigns. In stellarator design for fusion energy, direct interpolation of plasma boundary parameters can violate physical constraints even when both endpoints are feasible. Learned latent representations can capture nonlinear relationships among design variables, but latent interpolation can still cross infeasible regions, and conditioning on target metrics can become inconsistent with the decoded design. We introduce CHORD, a conditional variational autoencoder that penalizes predicted constraint violations along decoded latent interpolants during training, paired with self-consistent inference that aligns conditioning with the decoded design's predicted metrics. Geometric benchmarks show the benefit of regularizing latent interpolants. In stellarator interpolation between distinct geometry families, CHORD reaches up to 81% simulator-validated mid-segment feasibility, compared with 50% for an unregularized conditional VAE and 28% for direct interpolation of boundary parameters. Ablations show that both ingredients are needed for this gain. Beyond interpolation, latent-space optimization finds simulator-feasible designs, while self-consistent sampling produces more diverse feasible alternatives. On the ConStellaration benchmark, chord-regularized models with linear conditioning reuse data from five optimization campaigns and simulator-labeled rescalings to populate the Pareto front more densely. After low-fidelity screening, 93% of 1.2k generated candidates pass the benchmark's high-fidelity feasibility test. We release code and over 600k designs for stellarator genera

articles.title: Trust-Region Optimization for Performative Prediction without Response Modeling
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Performative prediction studies learning problems in which deployed decisions change the distribution of future data. Existing methods often impose structure on the population response, which limits their applicability when a fixed model class poorly captures that response. Generic black-box optimization avoids response modeling but does not exploit the known loss function. We introduce Performative Trust-Region Optimization (PTRO), which bridges these two approaches by optimizing performative risk without specifying or fitting a response model while still exploiting the known loss. The key idea is sampling from the current population to evaluate the known loss at nearby decisions, and use additional deployments only to estimate the effect of population response. This gives a local approximation of performative risk without committing to a model of how the population responds. PTRO then uses a trust-region mechanism to determine and adapt how far this local information can be trusted. Under moment-bounded losses and suitable smoothness and estimator-accuracy conditions, we establish high-probability convergence to an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the performative risk in $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ iterations, with $O(d^{3}\epsilon^{-4})$ samples per iteration, where $d$ is the decision dimension and $q\geq2$ is the loss-moment order. Experiments illustrate methods built around a specified response model can be more sample-efficient when their structural assumptions are accurate, whereas PTRO remains effective as the population response is poorly captured by a fixed model class. Ablations further show that both exploiting the known loss and adaptive trust-region updates are important for controlling the accuracy and efficiency.

articles.title: Near-Zero Forgetting Is Not Enough: Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Continual Learning of Pretrained VLAs
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work shows that pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit near-zero forgetting in specific continual learning settings with experience replay. However, robustness to domain shift of learned tasks remains unexplored. In this work, we study the robustness of Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under out-of-distribution (OOD) data using the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. While the in-domain (ID) setup achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting, OOD performance on previous tasks quickly collapses. Specifically, we show that during the continual learning process, the OOD capabilities of the model degrade, following a shared representational pattern across domain shifts, which is also visible behaviorally in the two simpler suites. Representational analysis shows that drift concentrates in the multimodal and action features. Linear probes indicate that OOD features still retain task-relevant information, but appear unreadable, consistent with representation misalignment. These findings suggest that even when ID stability remains intact, severe OOD forgetting can still occur, accompanied by representational drift during continual learning.

articles.title: How to build and train your recurrent-depth model: A fixed-point perspective
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation, yet it remains unclear why this works. We show that input injection, commonly used in recurrent-depth models, is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth. The guarantees require a Lipschitz operator, which for SwiGLU leads to a weight constraint in both row and spectral norm, while only a row norm constraint for gates. Based on these constraints, we develop an optimizer tailored to each parameter group, Sparrow, which provides a drop-in replacement of Muon/MuonH with no overhead, that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.

articles.title: SOTS: Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training data selection for machine learning models is a critical bottleneck in industrial applications where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing coreset selection methods for time series either ignore temporal structure entirely or cannot handle variable-length, irregularly sampled, multi-channel signals, the setting most common in industrial monitoring and testing. We introduce SOTS (Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection), an unsupervised coreset selection framework for irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) classification. Each sample is mapped to a truncated path signature, capturing the joint geometric structure of its channels, and the coreset is selected by greedily minimizing the Sliced Wasserstein distance between the empirical signature distributions of the candidate subset and the full dataset, a criterion for which we establish a convergence guarantee for random coresets. We validate SOTS on a real-world, highly imbalanced industrial I&C testing dataset, where SOTS-Greedy exceeds 95% of full-dataset accuracy using only 30% of the training data, outperforming standard coreset baselines at most budgets. This advantage generalizes to public UEA regular multivariate time series benchmarks specifically when class-discriminative information is purely geometric.

articles.title: Diagnosing Epistemic Uncertainty in Neural Operators: Effects of Initialization, Discretization, and Function Sampling
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but their reliability cannot be characterized by the performance of a single trained model. Existing neural operator uncertainty quantification approaches often characterize predictive uncertainty without separately identifying the contributions of individual sources of epistemic uncertainty. Finite sampling of the training function space, output discretization, and model initialization can produce substantial variation among learned operators even when the underlying physical problem is deterministic. We systematically investigate these sources of epistemic uncertainty across a diverse set of operator learning architectures. Across our experiments, we train approximately 46,000 neural operator models and construct ensembles over training datasets, model initializations, and output discretizations to characterize distributions of relative $L_2$ error rather than individual trained realizations. We find substantial architecture-dependent differences in epistemic uncertainty, with model initialization often accounting for the largest proportion of variance in relative $L_2$ error. The ranked performance of neural operator architectures can invert as the number and spatial distribution of output samples change, with the best architectures under sparse or randomly sampled observations differing from those at higher-resolution or structured discretizations. Furthermore, ensembles that reliably characterize aggregate operator error can provide unreliable estimates of error quantiles for individual test functions. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing the sources of epistemic uncertainty when evaluating neural operator reliabili

articles.title: ECLIPSE: Embedding-Centered Foundation-Model Federated Knowledge Transfer for Data-Free Edge Intelligence
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) are envisioned to become an integral component of intelligent federated edge networks because of their strong representation and generalization capabilities. However, their integration into resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive edge environments remains challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced in data-free settings, where no shared, public, or server-accessible reference dataset is available to establish a common reference space for aligning distributed knowledge. To address this challenge, we propose ECLIPSE, which is an embedding-centered FM-based federated knowledge transfer framework developed for data-free edge intelligence. ECLIPSE enables edge intelligence capitalizing on a server-hosted FM without sharing raw data, local models, or a public reference dataset. It establishes a shared embedding reference space through which edge devices encode their local task knowledge. Only the resulting embeddings are transmitted to the server for alignment and aggregation. Using the aggregated embeddings, the server constructs a task-aware surrogate dataset through an embedding-guided generative process. This surrogate dataset is then used to adapt the server-hosted FM to the downstream task. The adapted FM is subsequently distilled into a lightweight global model and distributed to the edge devices. This process allows edge devices to benefit from both distributed task knowledge and the generalization capabilities of the FM. Experimental results across diverse classification datasets show that ECLIPSE outperforms conventional Federated Learning (FL) and data-free Federated Knowledge-Transfer (FKT) baselines. It also achieves competitive performance compared with databased approaches. Fu

articles.title: JevBench: Metamorphic Coherence Testing for Typed Probabilistic Decision Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed probabilistic decision models return distributions over specified answers, such as yes or no, a set of options or levels on an ordered scale. We ask whether their probabilities remain coherent when questions about the same input are reworded, negated, combined, given different options or placed in different batches. JevBench tests this coherence without gold labels. Its 50 metamorphic relations each test one law of probability or choice across five dimensions: representation, batch independence, probability measure, logical order and choice-set conditioning. Each test changes the question or batch while keeping the input fixed. Every model receives the same requests, fixed in advance. JevBench-240 contains 12,000 tests across 240 synthetic cases in 12 decision domains. A fixed subset of 1,200 tests, JevBench-mini, closely reproduces the full-suite ranking (Spearman 0.983). Across 21 openly released models, coherence scores range from 56.5 to 83.9. Batch independence holds for most models. Additivity fails broadly, particularly for complements, where the probabilities of a proposition and its negation should sum to one. A uniform reference model ignores the input and scores 89.4 at chance accuracy, exceeding every evaluated model's coherence score. Among decoders, accuracy ranges from 82.4% to 89.2%, while coherence ranges from 64.2 to 83.9. These results show why both measures are needed to assess decision models. JevBench is available as an open-source Python package.

articles.title: Latent Channel Completion for Forecasting in Sensor Networks with Failed Detectors
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monitoring networks for traffic and utility infrastructure lose sensors routinely, and forecasting models that couple sensors together to gain accuracy also inherit an exposure to those losses. When a detector stops reporting, the substituted value is embedded as though it were a reading and propagates through the shared representation that couples the network, degrading forecasts for sensors that are still healthy. Because these models are selected on benchmarks where every sensor reports, the exposure is absent from the numbers used to choose them. We introduce Latent Channel Completion, a channel-axis joint embedding predictive objective that reconstructs missing sensors' latent representations rather than their values, since a coupling operator consumes embeddings and never sees raw readings. Channels are masked during training and their representations predicted from surviving channels against stop-gradient targets; at inference the operator fills in whichever sensors the monitoring system reports as dark, using parameters shared with the forecaster. On three highway detector networks, after half of each network goes dark, the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster, which on one network falls behind an uncoupled reference entirely. Against cross-channel ridge imputation drawing on the same surviving sensors, completing the latent lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6%, and on complete inputs, the method matches its backbone. The benefit tracks how much a network gains from coupling when intact, giving operators a criterion evaluable before any outage occurs.

articles.title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer. articles.title: Noise-Level Adjacency in Diffusion Training
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models train one network across all noise levels, although their training objective is pointwise in the noise level. If training on each pair of adjacent levels were an independent problem, separate networks with the same total parameter count would be expected to match one shared network. But in practice, on images, sharing weights across levels gives better results, which hints at an implicit dependence on their order. An order fixes both which levels are adjacent and the direction in which they run. In this paper, we show that, of the two, the benefit of sharing rests on adjacency in the noise-level embedding. The fitting error of a shared network is bounded below by the distances between neighbouring posterior means, minus the change the network can make between neighbouring embeddings. We first distinguish adjacency from direction: on a Gaussian mixture and CIFAR-10, reversing the embeddings keeps every neighbour and leaves the fitting error unchanged, whereas shuffling them raises it. Second, we rule out sharing between distant levels as the source of the benefit: separate networks on contiguous ranges match the shared network at its width, and with the parameters fixed, breaking adjacency at the same places costs less than 40\% of a full shuffle. Dividing the levels at equal shares of these distances lowers the error of all but the smallest networks. We therefore show that the order of the noise levels enters a diffusion model through adjacency, with its direction being a design choice. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/Noise-Level-Adjacency-in-Diffusion-Training.

articles.title: Eliciting sandbagged LLM capability via structural interventions on attention-head functional networks
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. Surprisingly, across model architectures and community detection methods, we find a consistent structural signature in which sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. We further demonstrate that this reorganization can guide capability elicitation. Ablating attention heads that exhibit the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving performance under honest behavior. Moreover, incorporating these structural signals further improves existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods. Together, our results show that sandbagging is accompanied by systematic reorganization of internal computation and demonstrate that functional network structure can provide both a mechanistic lens for understanding capability suppression and a practical signal for recovering hidden capabilities.

articles.title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

articles.title: Reward Basis Decomposition for Interpreting Preference Heterogeneity
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Canonical reward models specify the optimization target for AI policies, so understanding the values they encode is important for ensuring AI alignment. Existing interpretability techniques interpret reward models with a single reward head, which cannot distinguish between the values that a population shares and those that vary among individuals. We introduce Reward Basis Decomposition (RBD), which splits per-user weights into a population term and a per-user term. This yields a shared population direction and individual user directions that are analyzed separately via concept alignment and sparse autoencoder decomposition. We verify that RBD can recover artificially planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, then apply it to two real-world multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment. In both, we find no individual-user structure, suggesting that a single direction in the reward embedding space accounts for most preferences. We verify that RBD can recover artificially planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, then apply it to two real-world multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment. In both, we find no reliable predictive benefit from the fitted per-user terms beyond the shared population direction under our setup. Code and the synthetic dataset are available at https://github.com/RachelFreedman/RBD.

articles.title: Boundary Representation-Driven Graph Transformer Modeling for Machining Operation Sequencing
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machining process planning is inherently complex due to the interdependence between part geometry, machining operations, and evolving manufacturable states. Traditional approaches rely heavily on expert knowledge and rule-based systems, limiting scalability and automation. While recent machine learning methods have shown promise, most operate on simplified geometric representations, such as voxels or hand-crafted features, which fail to fully exploit the rich geometric and topological information encoded in Boundary Representation (B-Rep) models. In this work, we propose a graph transformer-based framework for geometry-to-sequence learning that directly predicts machining operation sequences from B-Rep design geometry. The proposed method constructs topology-aware graphs from B-Rep entities, where faces and their adjacencies are encoded as node and edge features capturing both geometric and relational information. A graph neural network encoder learns geometry-aware embeddings, which are then used to condition a dual-decoder transformer that autoregressively generates machining operation sequences. This formulation enables the model to capture both operation-type prediction and process-level ordering constraints directly from design geometry, without requiring intermediate feature extraction or machining-state representations. Experiments on a dataset of 2,991 synthetic machined parts demonstrate strong performance, achieving 95% accuracy for main operation prediction, 64% accuracy for sub-operation prediction, and 93% accuracy for sequence length prediction. Further analysis shows that the model effectively captures precedence relationships and geometry-dependent constraints inherent in machining processes. These results

articles.title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and disting

articles.title: Curvature-Equilibrated Policy Optimization for Deep Reinforcement Learning
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gradient-based actor optimization is central to deep reinforcement learning. However, conventional first-order optimizers do not explicitly exploit the local curvature of neural actor losses. We propose EQUIP (Curvature-Equilibrated Gradients for Policy Search), a novel approach that seeks to balance local contraction and expansion of the actor parameter space by equilibrating positive and negative curvature. EQUIP constructs a trajectory-informed search subspace and uses the projected Hessian of actor loss to build a bounded local metric for curvature equilibration. First-order loss matching preserves the approximated first-order decrease in actor loss. Meanwhile, gradient mixing and curvature-based gradient selection adjust the gradient applied for actor optimization. We establish the geometric properties of curvature equilibration, derive bounds on gradient alignment and magnitude, and identify conditions for improved actor loss reduction and convergence toward stationarity under direct gradient updates. We integrate EQUIP into Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) without modifying its actor loss, critic learning, or replay mechanism. Experiments on 6 MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks show that the resulting EQUIP-SAC algorithm achieves higher mean sample efficiency than SAC and two second-order policy optimization baselines. Ablation studies further highlight the benefits of curvature equilibration and trajectory-informed geometry for policy training.

articles.title: Tokenization and Architecture Jointly Allocate Component Roles in Time Series Transformers
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time series transformers have achieved strong forecasting performance, yet it remains unclear which of their components, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), constructs temporal features, and how tokenization such as patching changes this. We propose a temporal probing framework that uses 15 token-level diagnostic tasks to measure feature construction as the gain in linear decodability of temporal properties from one sub-layer to the next (a matched MLP probe already saturates at the embedding). It targets models whose probed representations are read by a linear forecasting head. Applied to 5 supervised models trained on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks, it finds that the constructing component is not fixed but allocated by the interaction of tokenization and architecture. Under patch tokenization (PatchTST), the FFN's gain exceeds attention's in probing on all 8 datasets, and its 8-dataset mean is 3.2x attention's. Without attention, the FFN alone reaches nearly the same total gain, both when attention is removed from a trained model and when PatchTST is trained without it, and the retrained model forecasts within a few percent of the full model. In probing, attention dominates under variate tokenization (iTransformer); in CATS, cross-attention is the only input path. In a controlled manipulation of PatchTST, single-scalar tokens (P=1) nearly eliminate the FFN's construction, while one more point per token (P=2) restores it. Our forecasting-side interventions (activation patching, knockout, and training without attention) establish component-level reliance and sufficiency. articles.title: Byte Patches versus BPE at Matched Data: A Matched-Twin Comparison at 350M Parameters
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31790v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We compare a MEGABYTE-style byte-patch Transformer with a 64-byte sliding local decoder (local64) to a matched byte-level 8k BPE decoder (BPE-8k) under identical raw bytes, document order, and approximately matched bytes per optimizer step: 350M parameters and 10 billion training bytes. Under matched-span document sliding (identical scored byte ranges), BPE-8k leads with relative gaps of -5.2%, -4.9%, -9.3% and -6.1% in bits per byte (overall, text, code, math; paired bootstrap). Downstream, CharBench equal fine-tuning favors local64 (53.7% vs 40.0%), fact200 favors BPE-8k (16.5% vs 7.0%), and PIQA (raw and length-normalized) and ARC-Easy length-normalized favor BPE-8k after Holm correction at alpha = 0.05; remaining tasks are ties. Evaluation pitfalls that changed conclusions include context-length extrapolation past the BPE training context, bits per token reported as bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators. Unlike controlled tokenizer studies that vary the subword tokenizer under a fixed token budget, or FLOP-controlled byte-model scaling studies, we hold the raw bytes, their order and the optimizer recipe fixed and ask whether a fixed-patch byte model can replace the tokenizer at all. Limits: one size, one seed, one 8k vocabulary fixed before the runs, and a known difference in embedding initialization between the twins.

articles.title: Start Where the Data Are: Statistical Priors for One-Step Generation on Manifolds
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast generation on manifolds is important for scientific applications such as protein design, yet existing one-step generators often produce spurious samples in low-density gaps between data modes. Our analysis highlights the mismatch between uniform noise and concentrated data, motivating a statistical prior that captures the data's coarse structure. We first estimate this prior by fitting mixtures of tangent-space Gaussians through geometry-aware moment matching. However, independent noise-data pairing can still connect different modes and weaken the benefit of the fitted prior. We therefore introduce posterior coupling, which samples a latent component conditioned on each data point and draws its paired noise from that component. To extend this approach to long torsion-angle chains, where full-covariance mixtures become costly, we use a hidden Markov prior to model sequential dependence with shared parameters. The resulting framework plugs into existing one-step training pipelines while retaining the generator architecture, training objective, and single network evaluation at inference. Experiments on spheres, tori, and SO(3) demonstrate substantial improvements across multiple generators, reducing distributional error by up to $125\times$ and the protein Ramachandran outlier rate from 12.1% to 0.55%.

articles.title: Subliminal Learning Crosses Modalities
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31870v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.

articles.title: Multi Agent Reinforcement Learning enhanced Federated Learning for Predicting Remaining Useful Lifetime
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction is central to Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). The growth of industrial IoT has unlocked large multivariate sensor streams and enabled deep models - especially Transformers - for long-horizon sequence learning. However, transformers are parameter-heavy and data-hungry, while operational datasets are often siloed and privacy-sensitive. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this by training across clients without raw data sharing, but in practice many clients connect over lossy wireless links where UDP is preferred for low latency, making model exchange vulnerable to packet drops. We present a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework that adapts FL to lossy channels by selecting per-client layer subsets to transmit and capping retransmissions. This framework is trained with QMIX value-function factorization for scalability. We instantiate the approach with a Graph Convolution Position-Aware Transformer (GCPATr) for RUL forecasting. On the CMAPSS dataset, our MARL-enhanced FL (RL-FL) consistently improves mean square error over standard FL, with the largest gains at high packet loss (e.g., up to 18% improvement on FD003 at 50% loss). These results show that MARL is an effective countermeasure to wireless degradation in FL-based RUL prediction.

articles.title: OrangeTree: A Linear and Tree-based Time Series Forecasting Model Supporting Multiple Input and Output Lengths
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.31905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) models suffer from a critical rigidity: the inability to handle Multiple Input and Output Lengths (MIOL) within a single architecture. Current workarounds, such as padding or autoregression, often incur computational redundancy or suffer from error accumulation. We propose OrangeTree, a linear and tree-based architecture that decouples model parameters from sequence lengths. It employs a Segment Tree Encoder and an Inverse Tree Decoder to translate multi-length input history into multi-length output predictions within a unified framework. Crucially, a Range Weighter and a Feature Fuser bridge these components, dynamically selecting and fusing relevant ranges into optimal contexts for forecasting. Experiments on six benchmarks confirm OrangeTree achieves the SOTA performance. In MIOL settings, it matches the accuracy of length-fixed models without substantial accuracy degradation or a substantial increase in inference latency typical of heuristic methods. Code is available at https://github.com/Tang-Yiqi/OrangeTree.
